opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think future prediction is really the heart of model predictive control. The basic idea in MPC is that you have a model of how the world evolves: given the current state and an action you might take, what happens next? Instead of just reacting to what you see right now, you roll that model forward a few steps, imagine several possible futures under different action sequences, score them against some objective, and then pick the best plan. Then, and this is the key part, you only execute the first action, observe what actually happened, and replan. So prediction isn't a one-shot forecast; it's a loop of imagine, act, correct.

What I find interesting is how this connects to what we're trying to do with world models in vision and AI more broadly. For a long time, a lot of computer vision was about recognition: you see an image, you label it. But if you want an agent that acts in the physical world, recognition isn't enough. You need some internal simulator that can answer counterfactual questions: if I push this cup, where will it go? If I turn left here, what will I see? That's exactly the predictive component in MPC, and I think a good visual world model is basically trying to learn that from data instead of hand-writing it with physics equations.

There's also a subtle point about what you predict. In classical control, you predict a low-dimensional state, like position and velocity, and that's well-defined. In the learned setting, people are tempted to predict pixels, the full future video frame. That's impressive, and generative video models are getting really good, but for planning you may not need every pixel. You need the parts of the future that matter for the decision. So I think the deeper question is about representation: can we learn a latent space where prediction is both accurate and useful for control? That's where a lot of ideas, like joint-embedding predictive approaches, become relevant: predict in an abstract representation space rather than reconstructing everything.

And finally, prediction gives you a form of robustness. Because you're constantly replanning, the model doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to be good enough over a short horizon, and feedback from reality corrects the errors. I think that's a healthy mindset for AI too: we don't need a perfect simulator of the universe, we need models that predict well enough, locally, to make good decisions, and that keep updating from real interaction.

r001.rationale: It says MPC rolls the model forward under different action sequences, scores the resulting possible futures against an objective, and picks the best plan.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says MPC executes only the first action, observes the outcome, and replans.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way to understand it is that in model predictive control, prediction isn't the goal, it's the instrument. The controller has a model of the world, it imagines what happens if it takes a sequence of actions, scores those imagined futures against some objective, picks the first action of the best sequence, executes it, and then throws everything else away and replans at the next step. So the predictive model exists to be queried for planning, nothing more.

That framing changes what you want from the predictor. In the pure generative world, people chase pixel fidelity. They want the video to look beautiful. But a controller doesn't care whether the texture of the wall is rendered correctly. It cares whether the model gets right the things that matter for the decision: will this object fall, will the gripper make contact, where will the car be in two seconds. That's really the argument behind what we've been calling world models with representations in the loop. You predict in a learned latent space where irrelevant details have been compressed away, and you keep only what's useful for anticipating consequences.

The second thing MPC teaches you is that prediction is allowed to be imperfect because the loop closes. You act, you observe the real outcome, you re-predict. So errors don't accumulate the way they do when you roll out a model open-loop for a long horizon. That's a very forgiving setting for learned models, and it's why I think it's a natural home for them. You need a model that is roughly right over short horizons and fast enough to query many times, rather than one that is perfectly right for a long time.

And then there's a deeper point I find interesting. Prediction becomes a form of understanding. If a model can anticipate how a scene evolves under its own interventions, it has implicitly learned something about physics, about causality, about affordances, without anyone labeling those things. In humans and animals this is arguably what perception is for in the first place. So when I think about future prediction in MPC, I don't see it as a control engineering detail. I see it as one of the clearest arguments for why visual representation learning and decision making should be built together rather than as separate stacks.

r001.rationale: It says the controller imagines outcomes for action sequences, scores those futures against an objective, and selects the best sequence.

r002.rationale: It says the controller executes the first action of the selected sequence, discards the rest, and replans at the next step.

astra-6.text:
I think future prediction is really at the core of model predictive control. Instead of reacting only to what’s happening right now, you use a model to ask: if I take this sequence of actions, how will the system evolve? Then you choose a sequence that best serves your objective while respecting constraints.

But the important part is that you don’t commit to that entire predicted future. You execute the first action, observe what actually happens, and plan again. So it’s a continual loop of prediction, action, and correction.

That also means the model doesn’t need to predict everything perfectly. It needs to capture the consequences that matter for the decision, over a useful horizon. If you predict too far ahead, errors can accumulate; if you look too little ahead, you can miss longer-term consequences. The challenge is to balance that foresight with uncertainty and keep grounding the plan in new observations.

r001.rationale: The response says the action sequence should best serve the objective, but does not explain that a cost is evaluated on model-predicted future states.

r002.rationale: It explains that only the first action is executed, then the system observes what happens and plans again.

sol-6.1.text:
I think future prediction is what allows model predictive control to act proactively. Instead of responding only to the current state, you use a model to ask: if I take this sequence of actions, how might the system evolve? Then you choose the sequence that best satisfies your objective while respecting constraints.

But you typically execute only the first action. You observe the new state and solve the problem again. That feedback loop is essential, because your predictions will never be perfect.

So the goal isn’t necessarily to predict the entire future with maximum accuracy. It’s to predict the consequences of different actions well enough to make a good decision now. A prediction error that changes which action you should take matters much more than one that doesn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says to use a model to consider how action sequences may affect the system, then choose one that satisfies the objective. It does not clearly state that a cost is evaluated on the model-predicted future states.

r002.rationale: It says to execute only the first action, observe the new state, and solve the problem again.
